title: Coding finite sequences: pairing and bounded decoding

based_on.title: Computability and Incompleteness
based_on.pages: 28–30 (§2.4, finite sequences, bounds, and simultaneous/history recursion; version 2007-01-09)

based_on.title: Formalizing Computability Theory via Partial Recursive Functions
based_on.venue: 10th International Conference on Interactive Theorem Proving (ITP 2019)
based_on.pages: 12:2–12:7 (§§2–3.1, square pairing and primitive-recursive data operations)

summary: Encode finite lists as natural numbers, prove explicit decoding bounds, and derive primitive-recursive list operations and recursion on finite histories.
abstract: An algorithm storing a list of natural numbers as a number must distinguish a missing entry from an entry equal to zero, and must be able to recover and manipulate the data. Repeatedly pairing natural numbers gives a code in which every number decodes to exactly one finite list, including the empty list. Removing a first entry strictly decreases the remaining code, so the code itself bounds a complete scan. Length, indexed access, reversal and concatenation can therefore be computed by primitive recursion, using prescribed finite iterations. The same representation lets one numerical state hold several changing values or the whole sequence of earlier results. With primitive-recursive update rules, this supports simultaneous updates and calculations that consult their history.
